title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 59–60
description: Curated B2 vocabulary on texture, light, density, physical weight, success, failure and difficulty; original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and relevant exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are independently written. Original passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

units.title: Unit 59 — Texture, brightness, weight and density
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 124–125 (PDF pages 125–126).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe tactile qualities with precise adjective choices such as rough, coarse, slippery, silky, jagged and prickly.
Choose natural combinations for surfaces, brightness, colour and light, including shiny, vivid, dazzling, dull, dim and glare.
Distinguish solid and hollow, thick and thin, fine hair, and dense and sparse vegetation.
Use expressions of weight and awkward size, including as light as a feather, as heavy as lead, bulky and cumbersome.

sectionsChecked: A: Adjectives and typical textures; tactile phrases with feel, surface, touch and underfoot
B: Brightness and colours; shiny and dazzling; glare and dim light
C: Solidity, thickness, vegetation density and weight similes
Exercises 59.1–59.5, including collocations and the answer key

items.example: The new notebook has smooth pages that are pleasant to write on.
items.note: Describes an even surface with no noticeable roughness.

items.example: The wooden table had a polished finish that reflected the light.
items.note: Often describes surfaces made smooth and shiny by treatment or rubbing.

items.example: The fabric felt surprisingly silky against her skin.
items.note: Smooth and soft, resembling silk.

items.pt: escorregadio; liso e difícil de segurar
items.example: Be careful on the slippery bathroom floor after your shower.
items.note: A slippery surface offers little grip, so you may slide or lose your hold.

items.example: The child chose a furry blanket for the sofa.
items.note: Covered in fur or something that feels like fur.

items.example: The wall was too rough for the adhesive tape to stick properly.
items.note: Describes a surface that is not smooth; often contrasts with smooth.

items.pt: grosso; de textura granulada ou áspera
items.example: The baker used coarse flour in the traditional bread.
items.note: Often refers to large particles or a rough texture, such as coarse sand or fabric.

items.example: The damaged metal panel had jagged edges that could cut someone.
items.note: Describes sharp, uneven or irregular edges rather than an entire smooth surface.

items.example: The prickly plant scratched my arm as I walked past it.
items.note: Something prickly has small, sharp points that can hurt to touch.

items.pt: toque sedoso; sensação sedosa ao toque
items.example: The expensive scarf has a silky feel despite being made of cotton.
items.note: Have a silky feel is a noun phrase for the tactile quality of material.

items.example: The ceramic cup is smooth to the touch, with no visible seams.
items.note: To the touch describes the sensation a material produces when handled.

items.example: The unpainted wooden shelf was rough to the touch.
items.note: A common phrase for describing texture from physical contact; reinforced in the exercises.

items.example: Dust was easy to notice on the polished surface of the desk.
items.note: A typical adjective and noun collocation for a treated, smooth surface.

items.example: The gravel felt uneven underfoot on the narrow path.
items.note: Used for the condition of the ground or surface one is walking on.

items.example: Although it was plastic, the handle had a surprisingly metallic feel.
items.note: The noun feel expresses a texture or sensation; found in an exercise on word forms.

items.example: We found a shady spot beneath the trees during the picnic.
items.note: Protected from direct sunlight; not the unrelated informal sense of suspicious.

items.pt: sombra; proteção contra a luz solar
items.example: The umbrellas provided welcome shade on the terrace.
items.note: A noun for shelter from direct sunlight; contrasts with the adjective shady.

items.example: The designer chose vivid blue and yellow for the poster.
items.note: Vivid colours are very bright and strong, rather than pale or dull.

items.example: Her freshly cleaned boots looked shiny in the morning light.
items.note: A reflective surface is shiny; the term need not mean intensely bright light.

items.example: A dazzling beam from the vehicle's headlights made it hard to see.
items.note: Very bright light that can briefly overwhelm your eyes; also figurative.

items.pt: apagado; sem brilho; de cor pouco viva
items.example: The old curtains were a dull brown that made the room seem gloomy.
items.note: For colours, means not bright or vivid; also has unrelated senses such as boring.

items.example: A bright orange sign stood out against the grey wall.
items.note: May describe strong light or vivid colour, depending on context.

items.example: The hallway was so dim that I could barely read the signs.
items.note: Used for weak light or a space with little illumination; contrasts with bright.

items.example: The glare from the low winter sun made driving uncomfortable.
items.note: Strong and unpleasantly bright light, often from the sun or reflections.

items.example: She bought a pair of shoes made from shiny black leather.
items.note: Natural combination for reflective leather surfaces.

items.example: A dazzling light appeared behind the stage when the show began.
items.note: Adjective and noun phrase for a light too bright to look at comfortably.

items.pt: proteger os olhos da luz com a mão ou outra barreira
items.example: He shaded his eyes with one hand to read the distant road sign.
items.note: Cover the eyes from direct sunlight or strong glare; exercise-context vocabulary.

items.example: The sculpture looks hollow, but it is made from solid stone.
items.note: In this contrast, solid means filled throughout rather than hollow.

items.example: The wooden column was hollow, so cables could pass through it.
items.note: Describes an object with empty space inside; contrasts with solid.

items.example: He has thick hair that takes a long time to dry.
items.note: Thick hair has a large amount of hair or substantial strands; contrasts with thin or fine.

items.example: She wore a thin jumper even though the room was cold.
items.note: Can describe thickness; thin hair is not abundant, and thin material is not thick.

items.example: A gentle brush can be helpful for people with fine hair.
items.note: Fine hair refers to individual strands that are thin, not necessarily sparse hair.

items.example: The research team struggled to walk through the dense forest.
items.note: Many things packed closely together; dense vegetation contrasts with sparse vegetation.

items.example: Only sparse vegetation grows on the dry hillside.
items.note: A small number of plants or objects spread over an area.

items.example: The portable sensor is as light as a feather compared with the old model.
items.note: A fixed simile meaning extremely light; clearly figurative.

items.example: The box felt as heavy as lead after the long walk home.
items.note: A fixed simile for something that feels extremely heavy; figurative.

items.pt: volumoso; grande e difícil de transportar
items.example: The bulky packaging took up most of the car boot.
items.note: Difficult to move or store because of its size; not necessarily very heavy.

items.pt: desajeitado; incômodo de transportar ou manusear
items.example: The old measuring device was too cumbersome for fieldwork.
items.note: Large, awkward or difficult to handle; can also describe complicated procedures.

items.example: Little vegetation survived the unusually dry summer.
items.note: Usually uncountable; frequently paired with dense or sparse.

items.example: The blanket remained soft to the touch after several washes.
items.note: An additional useful tactile collocation from the personal practice exercise.

items.example: You should polish the silver frame with a suitable cloth.
items.note: Verb for making an object smooth or shiny by rubbing; reinforced by the exercises.

units.title: Unit 60 — Success, failure and difficulty
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 126–127 (PDF pages 127–128).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use succeed in + -ing, manage to + infinitive and manage + direct object correctly.
Choose natural verbs and collocations for agreements, compromises, obligations, ambitions, dreams and targets.
Describe failures and setbacks with go wrong, backfire, fold, go under, falter and come to nothing.
Use patterns involving difficulty, trouble, bother and cope with, and recognise core word families for success and failure.

sectionsChecked: A: Success verbs, verb patterns and the goal/ambition/agreement collocation matrix
B: Failure and trouble; preposition and complement patterns; common countability mistakes
C: Word formation around succeeding and related roots
Exercises 60.1–60.5 and the answer key, including related word families

items.pt: conseguir; ter êxito em fazer algo
items.example: The researchers succeeded in reducing the error rate after several trials.
items.note: Use succeed in followed by a noun or -ing form, not succeed to do something.

items.pt: conseguir realizar algo, geralmente com esforço
items.example: We managed to finish the prototype before the demonstration.
items.note: Use manage to + infinitive for successfully doing something difficult.

items.pt: dar conta de; conseguir realizar uma tarefa
items.example: I can manage the short hike, but not the full mountain route.
items.note: Unlike succeed, manage may take a direct object meaning cope with a task.

items.example: The engineering team achieved its main objectives this quarter.
items.note: Especially natural with aims, targets and goals; can mean accomplish an outcome.

items.example: The volunteers accomplished a great deal over the weekend.
items.note: More formal than some alternatives; commonly takes a direct object or a quantity phrase.

items.example: The surprise celebration came off exactly as we had hoped.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for a plan or attempt succeeding.

items.example: After lengthy discussions, both departments reached an agreement.
items.note: A standard collocation for arriving at an agreement.

items.example: The negotiator secured an agreement that protected both sides.
items.note: Suggests successfully obtaining a sought agreement; slightly formal.

items.example: Every supplier must fulfil its contractual obligations.
items.note: Fulfil obligations or duties rather than typically reach them.

items.example: The company achieved its annual sales target earlier than expected.
items.note: Common business collocation: achieve a target, aim or goal.

items.example: We reached our fundraising target with two days to spare.
items.note: Reach a target also describes attaining a specified goal or amount.

items.example: The project attained its performance target in the final test.
items.note: Attain is a somewhat formal alternative to reach or achieve a target.

items.example: It took her years to attain her ambition of becoming a pilot.
items.note: Attain is relatively formal and can collocate with ambition.

items.pt: realizar uma ambição; concretizar uma aspiração
items.example: He realised his ambition to publish a novel before turning thirty.
items.note: British spelling realise; here it means make a cherished wish happen.

items.example: Winning the scholarship helped her fulfil a lifelong ambition.
items.note: Fulfil means bring a long-held ambition or goal to completion.

items.example: Opening her own studio allowed her to fulfil a childhood dream.
items.note: A frequent collocation for realising a deeply valued hope.

items.example: Their collaboration helped them realise their dream of developing a useful app.
items.note: Here realise means turn something imagined into reality, not notice or understand.

items.pt: chegar a um meio-termo; alcançar um compromisso
items.example: The two teams reached a compromise on the project deadline.
items.note: Reach a compromise is the preferred pattern in this unit's collocation matrix.

items.pt: realizar muita coisa; alcançar resultados expressivos
items.example: We achieved a great deal despite having only a small budget.
items.note: Achievement verbs can combine with quantity phrases such as a great deal or a lot.

items.pt: dar errado; não sair como planejado
items.example: The experiment went wrong when the temperature controller failed.
items.note: For plans or processes not proceeding as intended.

items.pt: sair pela culatra; produzir efeito contrário
items.example: The advertising campaign backfired and attracted harsh criticism.
items.note: Stronger than go wrong: an action creates an unwanted opposite effect.

items.pt: encerrar as atividades; fechar por dificuldades
items.example: The independent shop folded after several months of poor sales.
items.note: Businesses and organisations fold when they stop operating, often after failure.

items.example: Several small cafes went under during the economic downturn.
items.note: An informal way to say a business has failed and closed.

items.example: The recovery began to falter when costs rose unexpectedly.
items.note: Progress weakens or becomes uncertain; eventual failure is not inevitable.

items.pt: não dar em nada; fracassar completamente
items.example: Their plan to restore the theatre came to nothing when funding ended.
items.note: Describes efforts or hopes producing no successful result.

items.example: Many visitors have difficulty understanding the local transport map.
items.note: Use have difficulty + -ing or have difficulty in + -ing; usually uncountable.

items.example: I find it difficult to concentrate when several people are speaking.
items.note: Keep the object it before difficult when using find in this pattern.

items.example: The small text was hard to read from the back of the room.
items.note: Hard is a less formal alternative to difficult in this structure.

items.pt: ter problemas ou dificuldade para fazer algo
items.example: She has trouble connecting the laptop to the older projector.
items.note: Use have trouble + -ing; generally less formal than have difficulty.

items.example: We've had a lot of bother with the heating system recently.
items.note: In this sense, an informal uncountable noun for trouble or difficulties.

items.example: The team coped with the unexpected workload remarkably well.
items.note: Cope with a difficult situation; never omit with before the object.

items.pt: não conseguir lidar; não dar conta
items.example: With so many urgent tasks, he felt he couldn't cope any longer.
items.note: Used when demands feel too difficult to handle successfully.

items.example: The pilot project was a success, and the results were published.
items.note: Often uncountable for success in general: have success, not have successes here.

items.example: The smaller start-up succeeded because it listened to customers.
items.note: Verb corresponding to success and successful.

items.example: The first trial was successful, so the team repeated it.
items.note: Adjective in the succeed, success and successfully family.

items.example: The engineers successfully integrated the new sensor into the machine.
items.note: Adverb meaning in a way that achieves the intended result.

items.example: Completing the qualification was an important accomplishment for her.
items.note: Noun corresponding to accomplish; usually a successfully completed task.

items.example: She is an accomplished pianist who performs across Europe.
items.note: Adjective often means highly skilled, not merely that a task has been finished.

items.example: The new battery design was a significant achievement for the laboratory.
items.note: A result or accomplishment reached through effort.

items.example: The revised project deadline seems achievable with extra support.
items.note: An adjective meaning possible to achieve.

items.example: Educational attainment varies considerably between regions.
items.note: Noun for achieving a level, goal or qualification, often formal.

items.example: The objective is demanding but attainable within six months.
items.note: Something attainable can realistically be reached.

items.pt: realização; satisfação por atingir um objetivo
items.example: Teaching brought her a strong sense of fulfilment.
items.note: British spelling with one l in the middle; can mean satisfaction or completion.

items.example: He found mentoring younger colleagues very fulfilling.
items.note: Describes something rewarding that gives a sense of purpose.

items.example: The material will harden when it cools completely.
items.note: Verb in the hard, hardness and harden word family listed in the unit.

items.example: The technician measured the hardness of the metal sample.
items.note: Noun for the quality of being hard; not the same as difficulty.

items.example: The students worked hard to prepare for the final assessment.
items.note: Hard can function as an adjective or an adverb with the same spelling.

items.pt: realização de um plano; compreensão repentina
items.example: The realisation of the community project took more time than expected.
items.note: British spelling of the noun from realise; here means making something real.

items.example: The revised proposal is ambitious but still realisable.
items.note: British spelling of a possible-to-realise adjective; exercise word family.

items.example: She experienced great difficulty accessing the archived records.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring generally to problems doing a task.

items.example: The technical interview was difficult but fair.
items.note: Adjective paired with difficulty; there is no ordinary adverb difficultly.

items.pt: direcionado; destinado a um público específico
items.example: The charity introduced targeted support for rural communities.
items.note: Chosen or directed at a particular group; adjective in the target family.

items.example: The unexpected equipment failure delayed the measurements.
items.note: A lack of success or something breaking down; the noun of fail.

items.example: After two failed attempts, the team changed its approach.
items.note: Adjective often used for attempts, projects or plans that did not succeed.

items.example: The hospital had to replace its failing heating system.
items.note: Can describe a system or organisation whose performance is declining.

items.example: The audit identified several troubling safety issues.
items.note: Causes worry or concern; contrasts with troublesome.

items.example: A troublesome software defect kept delaying the release.
items.note: Causes repeated difficulty, inconvenience or problems.

items.example: She looked troubled after hearing the disappointing results.
items.note: Can describe a worried person or an organisation facing serious problems.

items.pt: invariavelmente; sem falhar; de forma constante
items.example: He was unfailingly polite to every visitor, even on busy days.
items.note: Unfailingly is possible; failingly is not a normal English adverb.

items.example: Her first research paper met with considerable success.
items.note: For achievement in general, success is uncountable; avoid successes in this sense.

items.example: The hikers crossed the flooded path with difficulty.
items.note: Natural adverbial expression; difficult has no ordinary direct adverb.

items.example: The small team completed the ambitious experiment against the odds.
items.note: Exercise-only phrase meaning despite the circumstances making success unlikely.
